title: Shaping results
summary: Compute new columns, rename them, and remove duplicates.

steps.title: Expressions and aliases
body: A column in `SELECT` can be any **expression**, and `AS` gives it a name:
- `||` joins text in SQLite, PostgreSQL and Oracle. SQL Server uses `+`; MySQL uses `CONCAT(a, b)`.
- `ROUND(x, 2)` rounds to two decimals. `UPPER`, `LOWER`, `LENGTH` work on text.
> **Watch out:** dividing two integers gives an integer in SQLite, PostgreSQL and SQL Server: `7 / 2` is `3`. Make one side a decimal (`7 / 2.0`) to get `3.5`.

steps.explain: Integer divided by integer throws away the remainder. `2.0` is a real number, so `7 / 2.0` is `3.5`. `%` gives the remainder, `1`.

steps.title: Labels with authors
prompt: Make labels for the Fantasy table. Return one column named **label** in the form `Title by Author`, for every `Fantasy` book.
For example: `The Lantern Keeper by Mara Ellison`.
Table: `books(id, title, author, genre, price, pages, year, stock)`
solution: SELECT title || ' by ' || author AS label

steps.title: DISTINCT
body: `SELECT DISTINCT` removes duplicate rows from the result:
SELECT DISTINCT author FROM books;          -- each author once
SELECT DISTINCT author, genre FROM books;   -- each (author, genre) pair once
DISTINCT applies to the **whole row** you select, not just the first column.

steps.title: Reviewing a teammate's query
body: Most SQL you read at work was written by someone else, and most SQL you write will be reviewed. A query that returns the right rows today can still be wrong for the job. Reviewers look for:
- **`SELECT *`** in application code or reports: it ships columns nobody asked for, and the result changes shape when someone adds a column. Name the columns.
- **The question the query answers.** "Authors with a cheap book" wants one row per author, not one row per book.
- **Conditions written the plain way.** `price < 10` says what it means; `NOT (price >= 10)` makes the reader stop and think (and behaves the same with NULL: both drop the row).
- **Layout.** One clause per line, keywords in one case, so the next person can see the shape at a glance.
Shorter is not the goal. Clear and correct is: the clever one-liner costs the next reader ten minutes.

steps.title: Review: authors with a cheap book
prompt: Rosa asks you to review this query before it goes into the promo email job. The ticket says: *"one row per author who has at least one book priced under 10, just the author's name"*.

It returns whole books (every column, and an author twice if they have two cheap books). Rewrite it to answer the ticket: a single column **author**, each author **once**, with the condition written plainly as `price < 10`.
Table: `books(id, title, author, genre, price, pages, year, stock)`

forbid.message: Names the column instead of SELECT *

hints: The ticket wants authors, not books: select only `author`.
An author with two cheap books should appear once: `SELECT DISTINCT author`.
steps.explain: Same rows the job needs, and a reader understands it in one look. `DISTINCT` is right here because the question really is "which authors"; when DISTINCT is used to hide duplicates a join created, that is a bug in the join, not a fix.
